ai_summary: Great Britain’s power system is demonstrating a stark geographical divide today, as Scottish electricity generation achieves an exemplary carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh versus 57 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. Across the wider national network, GB wind output has reached 12.7 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 2.3 GW, accounting for 22.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Despite this zero-carbon generation, cross-border transmission bottlenecks severely limit the export of power to southern demand centres. Consequently, 5,364 MWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring an immediate constraint cost of about £310,749. To maintain system security and replace this rejected renewable volume, gas-fired plants were ramped up downstream, resulting in an estimated 1,019,122 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and emitting 1,877 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualising these constraint expenditures yields an estimated total yearly cost of £113 million. When socialised across the wider energy system, this constraint burden results in an estimated increase of roughly £0.4/MWh on everybody's electricity invoice in the UK, underscoring the ongoing financial and environmental penalties of grid bottlenecks.
